messages.author: cdb8abc160f16f50
messages.subject: Yearly site covariates
parts:
Hello
I have a question for the interpretations for yearly site covariates for dynamic occupancy. Yearly site covariates, by definition, are the covariates that change per site as well as per year, right? And I guess it makes sense to use it to test colonization and extinction.
For example, I have relative abundance for coyote as a yearly site covariate and I'm using it to test colonization for bobcat. Let's say that I found coyote yearly abundance had a strong positive impact bobcat colonization. Does it mean that sites with higher coyotes are going to attract more bobcats to move it or does it mean that in years with coyote being more abundant, there'll be more bobcats moving in?
Xinzhu

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Yearly site covariates
parts:
Dear Xinzhu,

I think that it is neither of the two: in your two proposed interpretations you seem to imply a site or a year covariate.

But we are talking about a site-year covariate. Finding that coyote yearly abundance has a strong positive impact on bobcat colonization means this: when a site has zero bobcats in one year, then it is more likely to have at least one bobcat in the next year if it has a higher value of the coyote abundance covariate. So, it's not a comparison between one set of sites and another (those with lots of coyotes and those without) or one set of years and another, but between one set of site-year combinations with another.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.author: cdb8abc160f16f50
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Yearly site covariates
parts:
Hi Marc:
Thanks. First, I want to make sure that we are on the same page regarding what we mean by "year-site covariate". I was talking about covariates that vary both site and year. So, I have different value per site and per year. (See attached, all the valued are Z-scored). Were you thinking about the same thing?

 

Actually, I think I haven't paid much attention to the interpretation of different covariate in dynamic occupancy models. For example, we also have site-level covariates. Like, percentage of forest. If forest have a positive impact on bobcat colonization, does it mean that if a site has no bobcat in year 1, it's likely to have at least one bobcat in year 2 if a site has higher proportion of forest? And we also have survey-level covariates. For example, temperature. If temperature has a negative impact on detection in dynamic occupancy models, does it mean that with higher temperature in a survey period (e.g, a week), bobcats are less likely to be detected in that week?

Best,

Xinzhu
